runs.selected_topic: 2-edge-connected components and the bridge tree: two edge-disjoint routes, the contraction, and the leaves that set the augmentation
runs.selected_microtopic: a bridge as an edge on no cycle and the deletion test; the relation 'u = v or two edge-disjoint routes join them' and its transitivity by gluing routes; the classes as the pieces left after cutting bridges; the bowtie, where 'lies on a common cycle' is not transitive (1~0 and 0~3 but not 1~3) yet the graph is one 2-edge-connected component and two blocks; one depth-first search from the hub of a fourteen-station graph with its real disc and low values (6,5,4,3,2,1,0 then 7..13; lows 5,5,5,2,2,2,1,8,8,8,8,12,12,12); the test low[child] > disc[parent] strictly, with station 5 and child 4 giving low 2 against disc 2 and NOT a bridge; skipping the parent EDGE by identity, where two parallel edges give truth 0, edge-id 0 and parent-vertex 1; contracting the four bridges to a five-node bridge tree with degrees 1,2,3,1,1; the count identity 5 = 1 + 4; bridge-tree distance as the number of bridges on a route; the augmentation ceil(L/2) = 2 for three leaves, not the 3 that counting degree-one stations gives, plus ceil(p/2) + q for a disconnected graph; and the three confusions: bridge against articulation point (K2, bowtie), 2-edge against 2-vertex connectivity, and the undirected against the directed decomposition

Rule 5 applies too, because the bridge forest is the structure that answers every single-link-failure question at once, and the previous run's second candidate (a revision pass over the four earliest lessons) is left for a run that is not adding a lesson. No marks distribution is claimed.

bridge against articulation point, in both directions (K2 and the bowtie)

runs.selected_unit: Asymptotic worst case time complexity (sorting) - GATE 2027 Section 5
runs.selected_topic: The comparison lower bound: decision trees, leaf counting and the exact height
runs.selected_microtopic: the algorithm drawn as a binary tree of comparisons (internal node = one comparison, one run = one root-to-leaf path, worst case = height); n! leaves needed because a correct sort must separate n! input orders; a tree of height h has at most 2^h leaves, counted over all 677 shapes of height at most 4; the ceiling of log2(n!) computed in whole numbers for n = 1..22; why the ceiling is forced (2^6 = 64 < 120 at n = 5) and why the base is two (the equality outcome cannot occur for distinct keys); the exact minima for n = 3..6 recomputed by exhaustive minimax (3, 5, 7, 10) and their agreement with the ceiling; the merge-insertion sandwich ceil(log2 n!) <= S(n) <= sum ceil(log2 3k/4), met for every n up to 11 and missed at n = 12 (29 against 30), with a gap that is not monotone (0 again at 20 and 21, 1 again at 22); Stirling in base two and the Theta(n log n) conclusion, with the merge sort closed form checked against a simulation; the average floor log2 L for a tree with L leaves, measured on the built n = 4 tree (4.667) and against insertion sort (4.917 average, 3 best); and the escape route, counting sort making zero comparisons
runs.priority_reason: Rule 1 (repair) did not apply: a fresh clone was clean at the previous run's published commit, syllabus-coverage.json held 144 entries all PUBLISHED with no IN_PROGRESS or NEEDS_REVIEW entry, and the working tree held nothing unfinished. Every named clause of Sections 1-10 already had an owner among the 144 lessons, so the run fell to rules 4, 5 and 6, and the gap was found by asking what an existing lesson states but never computes. The previous run's own log named this as the strongest remaining candidate in exactly those words: the arithmetic of the comparison lower bound and its decision tree, the exact number of leaves, the ceil(log2 n!) bound and the tightness for small n, where the sorting lesson states the bound but the leaf-count arithmetic is only partly computed. Reading the neighbours confirmed it: topics/sorting-algorithms prints the bound as one line and builds a decision tree for three keys in one scene but never tabulates the ceiling, never states an exact minimum, never distinguishes the floor from the achievable minimum, and never computes the average floor; topics/selection-lower-bounds-max-min-second-largest owns exact comparison counts for the maximum, the maximum-and-minimum together and the second largest, which is a different problem with a different adversary argument. Rule 6 also applied: this is the misconception-dense microtopic of the sorting unit (rounding down, base three, floor read as minimum, floor read as best case), and each has a smallest case that kills it. Rule 4 applied too: three previous-year items ask it directly (1991, 2004, 1990), and no lesson in the repository cited any of them. No marks distribution is claimed.

runs.selected_microtopic: a node as a value plus the address of the next one, so index arithmetic becomes a stored-address chase; the self-referential struct, NULL as terminator, padding in sizeof, and a length that is stored nowhere; insert after p in two writes and the mandatory order (x->next = p->next, then p->next = x) with the wrong order making the tail unreachable; GATE 1998 Q19a traced by addresses rather than arrows, including the fourth line's (p->next)->next; delete after p in one write with the victim saved first; the head pointer being the list, why a by-value head parameter cannot report a new first node, and the three repairs (return the new head, node **, dummy header); GATE 2010 Q36 move_to_front with detach-attach-move as the only safe order and why B and C fail; the array-versus-list cost table row by row, with binary search impossible on a list and insert at position k linear in both for different reasons; delete the node you were given as O(n) singly against O(1) doubly (GATE 2023 Q03, GATE IT 2004) and why the copy-the-successor trick cannot rescue the worst case because it has no move for the last node; the doubly linked invariant b->next->prev == b and b->prev->next == b, the four-write middle splice against the two-write singly splice, and two-write deletion from a node pointer; GATE 2016 Set 2 Q15 with the decrease-key term dominating; circular lists with no NULL, the stopping rule you must supply, GATE 2004 Q36 pointing the single pointer at the rear, and GATE 1997 Q1.4 concatenating in four writes via head->prev; reversal with three cursors, next saved before the overwrite, n link writes in n steps, O(1) space (GATE 2022 Q05) against the recursive version's linear stack; merging two sorted lists in place with at most n1+n2-1 comparisons and no new nodes; Floyd cycle detection with the mu + lambda bound, the meeting node not being the entry, and the computed case mu = 5, lambda = 3 meeting after 6 steps; and a four-question procedure (is a pointer given, which fields change, is the head changing, is the list circular) with GATE 2017 Set 1 Q08 and GATE 2003 as the confirming shapes.

corrections_made_during_this_run: The model was written and run standalone before any drawing code existed. Prim's tie-break initially returned the same edge set as Kruskal, which would have made the 'same weight, different tree' scene false, so the rule was changed to 'on equal keys take the later label' and is stated on screen; Prim now takes A-C where Kruskal takes A-B, both totalling 24.

Dijkstra was first implemented relaxing into already-settled vertices, which made the negative-edge example report the correct distance to A by accident. It now refuses to relax a settled vertex, which is the commitment the algorithm actually makes, and the example shows two wrong values (A 1 against 0, T 2 against 1).

The 2016 Set 1 Q38 check first asked whether the x-edge was used by a single-source run, which is the wrong criterion; it now computes the best route that avoids the edge with Floyd-Warshall and asks whether the direct edge ties it, giving 12.
Floyd-Warshall was initially given one direction per edge on the undirected 4-vertex instance, so it reported infinity and then 20 for the largest x. Both directions are now inserted.

Two model checks were themselves wrong and were fixed: the DFS interval test was not symmetric, so every ancestor-descendant pair was flagged; and the four-vertex uniqueness check asserted weight 22 where the enumeration gives 12 (2 + 5 + 5).

A variable named K for the Kruskal result shadowed the lesson-kit handle K, so the page threw on boot ('K.init is not a function'). The Kruskal result is now KR; the checker caught this, not the browser.
The geometry audit found 27 text-on-text collisions; eight scene layouts were rebuilt and the audit is now clean.

corrections_made_during_this_run: The model was written and run standalone in Python before any drawing code existed, and two bugs were caught there rather than in the browser: the generate bit was computed as (a >> i) & 1 & b, which Python parses as a & (1 & b), so every generate bit was wrong; and the unrolled carry multiplied one propagate term too many for the last summand, so the unrolled formula disagreed with the recurrence.

The delay model was restated. The lesson first claimed the textbook 'carry 2n, last sum 2n + 1', which the page's own depth model does not produce: with the external carry in arriving at level 0, the carry out of column i costs two levels and a sum bit one more, so the last sum bit settles at 2n - 1, one level BEFORE the final carry. The model function rippleDepths() was written, the claim was replaced everywhere it appeared (timeline, GATE patterns, revision sheet) and the check now derives both numbers for n = 1..32. A check that asserted 2n = 2n was also removed: it proved nothing.

The hazard simulator first evaluated every gate from the current level's values, which is a zero-delay evaluation and produced no glitch at all (trace 1 1 1 1 1 1). It now reads the previous level, and the trace is 1 1 1 0 1 1.

The hazard check was written against a five-level trace; the corrected simulator emits six levels, so the assertion was rewritten as an invariant (exactly one zero, at level 3, with 1 on both sides) rather than a magic string.
A duplicated assignment in addSub computed the complemented operand twice, the first time with a precedence bug; the dead line was removed.

microtopics_covered: schema vs instance; degree (arity) vs cardinality
a relation is a set, so a duplicate tuple cannot exist - the fact SQL deliberately breaks
the six primitives and which operators are derived
selection keeps rows and leaves the schema; projection keeps columns and drops duplicates
pi on CR: 18 printed tuples collapse to 4 distinct courses; the bag projection keeps 18
pi is SELECT DISTINCT, sigma is WHERE - SELECT alone is bag projection
union, difference and intersection need identical schemas in the same attribute order
intersection as R - (R - S); difference is one-directional
|R x S| = |R| * |S| and degree(R x S) = degree(R) + degree(S)
theta join as a selection on a product, keeping both joined attributes
natural join keeps one copy: degree = sum of degrees minus the common attributes
a natural join with no common attribute equals the Cartesian product
outer joins are SQL, not algebra, and are why NULL has two meanings
division as the algebra's 'for every'; the answer has fewer attributes than the left operand
GATE 2017 Set 1 Q46: T1 = {CA, CB, CC} and CR / T1 = {SA, SC, SD, SF}, 4 rows
SB lacks CA and SE lacks CC; one missing course is enough
R / S = pi_A(R) - pi_A(pi_A(R) x S - R), with no selection in it
division by an empty S returns every A-value of R, by vacuous truth
the division expression is illegal unless S's attributes are a subset of R's
GATE 2022 Q25: A and B are both correct; C returns {E1} on witness 1 and D returns {E1,E2} on witness 2
C divides by the projection of the fact table, dropping brands nobody owns
D forms every employee-brand pair before dividing, inventing ownership
one witness kills an option; the printed instance is not a proof
tuple relational calculus as a set former; free and bound variables; safety
a variable shared by two relations becomes an equality join condition, decided by position
a quantified variable that is not reported is projected away
GATE 2026 Set 1 Q43: E = pi_P(S join on S.X = R.Q R), option B, and the other three return nothing
SQL evaluation order FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY
an alias made in SELECT cannot be used in WHERE; an aggregate cannot appear in WHERE
HAVING filters groups, never rows
the operator correspondence, and that EXCEPT/INTERSECT are not in every engine
UNION removes duplicates while UNION ALL keeps them
NULL as a third truth value; WHERE keeps only TRUE; NOT UNKNOWN is UNKNOWN
NULL AND FALSE is FALSE; NULL OR TRUE is TRUE; NULL AND TRUE is UNKNOWN
on x = {6, 5, NULL}: x = 5 returns 1 row and x <> 5 returns 1 row, so 2 not 3
the law of the excluded middle fails on NULL rows
GATE 2000 Q2.26: under the paper's stipulation, pair C is not equivalent; under 3VL none of the three differ
NOT IN over a subquery holding a NULL returns 0 rows; NOT EXISTS returns 2 here
COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts values; AVG divides by the non-NULL count
all rows whose grouping key is NULL form one group; HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 keeps 2 of 3
a join condition never matches two NULL keys
ER mapping: 1:N puts the foreign key on the many side and needs no relation of its own
M:N needs its own relation keyed by the pair of foreign keys
multivalued attributes and weak entities each need their own relation; a weak key is owner key plus partial key
the worked ER example produces six relations

a table can refute a candidate dependency and can never establish one
trivial, non-trivial and completely non-trivial dependencies

reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity as the complete axiom set

minimal cover by splitting right sides, dropping extraneous left attributes and redundant FDs

1NF as atomicity, which a set-valued attribute fails before any FD is examined

the implication chain BCNF => 3NF => 2NF => 1NF and the failure of every converse

the two-fragment test and its failure when the shared set is empty

dependency preservation by projecting F onto each fragment and re-deriving F
a dependency spanning two fragments may still be implied by their union
GATE 2001 AB|CD: dependency preserving and lossy at once
GATE 2001 Q2.23: 14 partitions enumerated, none BCNF, lossless and preserving

a decomposition can be BCNF and preserving while still being lossy

microtopics_covered: a node is a block, so cost is a count of block reads
blocking factor = floor(block size / record size)
heap, sequential and hashed file organisation
dense index (one entry per record) versus sparse index (one entry per block)
sparse indexing requires a file sorted on the key
clustered versus unclustered index, on the same axis as primary versus secondary
multilevel index and the top level staying in memory
order p = maximum children, so p-1 keys and p pointers
minimum degree form: max keys 2t-1, min keys t-1 for a non-root node
minimum keys = ceil(order/2) - 1, with the root exempt
B-tree: record pointer in every node, each key once, a search may end at an internal node
B+ tree: record pointers only at the leaves, so every search costs the height
copy-up rule: separator = smallest key in the subtree to its right
leaf chain, and why a range scan never returns to the root
internal-node byte equation p*ptr + (p-1)*key <= block
leaf-node byte equation n*(key+recptr) + exactly one chain pointer <= block
the order is always a floor; rounding up produces a node that does not fit
insertion: descend, insert, split on overflow, copy up, propagate
a root split is the only event that increases the height
deletion: remove, then borrow from a sibling with spare keys, then merge
underflow repair cascades upward; a root with no keys contracts to its only child
a point query costs the height; a range query costs the height plus the extra leaves
count nodes fetched, not keys compared
an open upper bound still costs the last leaf it touches
levels and disk accesses including the final record block
height bounds: max keys (p-1)p^(h-1) and min keys ceil(p/2)^(h-1)*(ceil(p/2)-1)
B-tree against B+ tree on one key set: levels, key slots, scan shape
duplicate search keys break the separator rule, so index keys are made unique
an empty tree is a single empty leaf at height 1

GATE CSE 2014 Set 2 Q35 - accepting a string of length 2014. Recognisable by dovetailing over finitely many strings of that length, not decidable because the property is semantic: answer B.
GATE CSE 2013 Q17 - four statements about closure and determinism. Only statement 2 is false, on the complement half, which the closure table and Post's theorem both show.
GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q13 - what 'M decides L' is equivalent to: accepting every string in L and rejecting every string outside it. Used as the definition the fates scene rests on.
GATE CSE 2014 Set 3 Q16 - Sigma* countable, its power set uncountable: the premise of the counting scene, which computes 31 strings against 2^31 languages.

runs.selected_microtopic: four quantities and the questions they answer. runs.selected_unit: Aptitude — Section 2, Quantitative Aptitude
runs.selected_topic: Quantitative aptitude: data interpretation, numerical computation and estimation, mensuration and geometry, elementary statistics and probability
runs.selected_microtopic: five computations rather than four headings. (1) Share of one base: Rs 1, Rs 5 and Rs 10 coins in 5:3:13 have values 5, 15 and 130, so the base is Rs 150 and not the 21 coins, and Rs 15 of Rs 150 is 10 per cent (GATE CSE 2024 Set 1 GA Q4, official key C), with both wrong bases computed — 3/21 = 14 2/7 per cent from a count over a count, and 15/50 = 30 per cent from a part over the wrong part. (2) The chain: 45 per cent of 2,000 kcal is 900 kcal, and 900 over 9 kcal per gram is 100 grams of fat, with the sector angles checked to close at 360 degrees and the five energies to sum to 2,000 (Q8, key C); grouping is exact only because all three fats share one density, which the page asserts by computing both the grouped and the per-row answer. (3) The identity: log(ab) = log a + log b turns log(p^2+q^2) = log p + log q + 2 log 3 into p^2+q^2 = 9pq, and squaring keeps the middle term, giving (p^4+q^4)/(p^2 q^2) = 79 and not 81 (Q5, key A), confirmed numerically at both roots of r^2 - 9r + 1 = 0. (4) The shape: joining the two 54 cm edges makes 54 the height and 4 the distance around, so the tube is 216/pi against a cube of side 6 and volume 216, and the ratio is 1/pi (Q7, key A); the other reading of the fold gives 13.5/pi and using the circumference as a radius gives 4/pi, which is an offered option. (5) The centre and the count: sorted, the sample has median 13.5 and mean 18.7 with five of ten values above the median and never more (Q3, key A; the statement GATE CSE 2023 GA Q4 asked for), and removing the 69 drops the mean to 13.11 while the median stays at 13; three tosses give eight outcomes with one complement, 7/8, and five red against three blue without replacement give 28 pairs with 3 both blue, 25/28 against 55/64 with replacement. (6) The recurrence: 37 and 60 run backwards give 23, 14, 9, 5, 4 and F1 = 4, checked by one forward pass (GATE CSE 2023 GA Q3, key A). (7) Estimation: 2^10 = 1024 is a 2.4 per cent error against a thousand, 1.05^14 = 1.9799 and 1.05^15 = 2.079 bracket the doubling, and 72/5 = 14.4 agrees within a year.

runs.selected_unit: Databases — Section 9, the ER model
runs.selected_topic: The entity-relationship model and its mapping to the relational model: entity sets and attribute kinds, relationship sets and degree, cardinality ratios, participation constraints, weak entity sets and identifying relationships, specialisation and generalisation, and the mapping rules
runs.selected_microtopic: Six tables, and every count derived rather than quoted. (1) Shapes: rectangle entity, capsule attribute, diamond relationship, and a double border that means a different construct on each of the three. (2) Ratio as a count: the page enumerates all 2^(mn) subsets of the grid of pairs and filters them by the constraint, then compares with the closed form — M:N on 3x2 gives 64 = 2^6, 1:1 gives 13 = sum C(3,k)C(2,k)k!, 1:N with 3 on the one side and 4 on the many gives 256 = (3+1)^4. (3) Participation is a second, independent constraint: the same 1:N pair on 2 and 3 gives 27, 8, 12 and 6 instances as the two sides become total in turn; 1:1 with both sides total on 3 and 2 gives zero, because a perfect matching needs equal sizes, while total on the two-entity side alone gives P(3,2) = 6. (4) Nullability: total participation gives 0 nulls in 5 copies and 3 branches, partial gives 2 nulls in 5 readers; GATE CSE 2017 Set 2 Q17 is exactly this argument, and GATE CSE 2018 Q11 is many-to-one plus total, checked over all 6 instances of a 2x3 version, where no E1 entity ever has two partners and the largest E2 load is always at least 2. (5) Weak keys: 6 copies share 2 copy numbers, so 4 collisions, and (isbn, copy_no) gives 6 keys and none; the identifying relationship makes no table (GATE CSE 2024 Set 2, GATE CSE 2020 Q14). (6) ISA: strategies A, B and C give 3, 1 and 2 tables, and C stores 3 persons as 4 rows once the subclasses overlap. (7) The seven rules run over a library schema give exactly Reader, Book, Branch, Copy, Borrows and Reader_Phone — 3 strong + 1 weak + 1 M:N + 1 multivalued — with bid inside Copy, rid inside Branch, and neither Keeps nor Manages making a table; rejoining Borrows to Copy recovers all 5 universal rows, while folding the M:N into Reader keeps 3 and loses 2. (8) The same mapper reproduces GATE CSE 2015 Set 1 Q38 (4 relations, a11 in E3), 2008 Q82 (3 tables, and {M1,M2,M3,P1} for M) and 2005 Q15 (3 tables), so those keys are derived from the rules rather than remembered.

runs.selected_unit: Algorithms — Section 5, algorithm design techniques
runs.selected_topic: Divide and conquer: the three-step pattern, the recursion tree, the master-theorem cases, decrease and conquer, and the exact counts behind merge sort, quicksort, binary search and Karatsuba
runs.selected_microtopic: One technique counted four ways. (1) Shape: divide into a parts of size n/b, conquer, combine at f(n), with the recurrence read off the code rather than remembered. (2) Tree: merge sort at n = 8 built as a tree and counted - 3 levels, 8 leaves, 7 merges, level sums 8,8,8,8 and 24 units of work, the leaf level excluded from the total because it does no merging. (3) Case: five recurrences evaluated by direct recursion at n = 256 and matched to closed forms - 2T(n/2)+n = 2304 = n log2 n + n, 2T(n/2)+n^2 = 130816 = 2n^2-n, 4T(n/2)+n = 130816 = 2n^2-n (the same number by a different case), 2T(n/2)+1 = 511 = 2n-1, 8T(n/2)+n^2 = 33488896 just under 2n^3 - plus the leaf identity a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) checked as an integer equality: 3^8 = 6561 = 256^1.585. (4) Count: all 40,320 orderings of eight elements sorted by merge sort and by quicksort - merge worst 17 = n ceil(lg n) - 2^ceil(lg n) + 1, best 12, average 15.73; quicksort worst 28 = n(n-1)/2 on both sorted and reverse-sorted input, best 13, average 16.92 = 2(n+1)H_n - 4n; every interleaving of two sorted lists for all m,n up to 4 giving exactly min(m,n) and m+n-1; binary search on every size up to 64 and every target giving floor(lg n)+1; Karatsuba 3^k against schoolbook 4^k with the crossover computed (9 against 8 at n = 2, 39 against 48 at n = 4); and the maximum-subarray recursion returning 29 on the GATE CSE 2019 Q25 array, agreeing with brute force over all 105 ranges and on 200 seeded random arrays.

runs.selected_unit: Analysis - the counting skill behind Section 5 and Section 3
runs.selected_topic: Exact counts across the syllabus: comparisons, probes, block transfers and multiplications
runs.selected_microtopic: Four units and one four-step procedure, with seven instances. (1) Merge sort at n = 8 is 24 units of work and 17 comparisons, and the gap is the 7 merges; the closed form n ceil(lg n) - 2^ceil(lg n) + 1 is checked against the enumeration of all 40,320 orderings at every n from 1 to 8 (0, 1, 3, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17 both ways). (2) Quicksort: n - 1 per partition, worst n(n-1)/2 = 28, average 2(n+1)H_n - 4n = 16.92, best 13; GATE CSE 2014 Set 1's two inputs are 10 and 6, so t1 > t2 - and the first partition ties at 4, which is why only a total count sees the difference. (3) Binary search floor(lg n) + 1, verified for every size to 64 and every target, successful and unsuccessful; at n = 1024 that is 11. GATE CSE 2007 Q15's doubling loop is executed for every n to 64 and matches floor(lg n) + 1, with ceil(lg n) + 1 shown to fail at n = 15 (5 against 4). (4) A seven-slot chained table of ten keys: 14 probes over 10 keys = 1.4 successful, 17 over 7 slots = 2.43 unsuccessful, against the estimates 1 + alpha/2 = 1.71 and alpha = 1.43 - the table lands on both sides, which is what an average over hash functions means. Open addressing 1/(1-alpha) is 2 at alpha = 0.5 and 10 at alpha = 0.9, the figure GATE DS&AI 2024 Q11 asks for. (5) Sixteen cache accesses, block of four words, two blocks: 4 transfers row-major and 16 column-major, so AMAT is 11 against 41 cycles at a one-cycle hit and a 40-cycle penalty. (6) Matrix chain at n = 5: 10 cells (n(n-1)/2) and 20 transitions (n(n^2-1)/6), checked at every n from 2 to 10; LCS at 4 by 5 is 30 cells. (7) Karatsuba 3^k against 4^k, exponent 1.585, 59049 against 1048576 at n = 1024, with the leaf identity checked as a near-equality. Scene 9 puts all four units on one n: 11, 10240, 256 and 59049.

runs.verification_note: No database engine was executed: the build environment had no server, so no behaviour is quoted as live output. runs.selected_microtopic: a representation as a price list rather than a format: one undirected edge costs two cells in a matrix and two entries in a list, so seven edges give 14 ones and 14 chain entries on the same six-vertex graph; the matrix is sized by n alone (36 cells, 5 bytes packed, 144 bytes as 32-bit integers) and the list by n and m together (4n + 16m bytes, so 136 here and 36,000 at n = 1000, m = 2000, against 125,000 packed); the list overtakes the packed matrix only while m < 7,562 at n = 1000, and never at n = 6, so 'lists are smaller' is a claim about density; the matrix sells an O(1) edge test and pays Theta(n) to enumerate neighbours, which is why a whole traversal is 36 cell reads against 20 list steps and why the tightest bound on DFS with a matrix is Theta(n^2) (GATE CSE 2014 Set 1); twin pointers in an undirected list cost Theta(n + m) with a table and O(m^2) with a nested scan (GATE CSE 2016 Set 2 Q41); A^k counts walks of length k, so the diagonal of A^2 is the degree sequence (GATE CSE 2022 Q10), the sum of A^2 is the sum of the squared degrees (36 here) and trace(A^3)/6 is the triangle count (GATE CSE 2022 Q12), six because a triangle is walked from three corners in two directions, while A = A inverse forces every degree to 1 and hence a perfect matching (GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q7); the incidence matrix has two ones per column, rank n - c over GF(2) and nullity m - n + c = 2 = the cycle count, but real rank 6 rather than 5 because the graph is not bipartite; and K3,3 versus the triangular prism, both 3-regular on six vertices with nine edges and 0 against 2 triangles, shows that a degree sequence never decides a graph

runs.selected_topic: Bayes' theorem as a revision rule: the prior, the likelihood, the evidence computed as a sum over the hypotheses, and the posterior — with the base-rate case, the odds form, sequential updating, multi-hypothesis questions with unequal priors, the two conditional directions, the partition requirement, and the four places the rule stops applying
runs.selected_microtopic: the evidence as a sum, and the three things that follow from it. Five coins, four regular and one fake, give prior 0.20, likelihoods 1 and 0.25, paths 0.20 and 0.20, evidence 0.40 and posterior 0.50 — the 2025 CSE answer. The same sum is 0.55 for the shop's bulbs (CSE 2016 Set 2, no division afterwards) and 0.75 for the noisy channel, where 0.03 over 0.75 is 0.04 (CSE 2021 Set 1 Q54). At 1 per cent prevalence a 99 per cent accurate test gives exactly one half, counted as 99 ill and 99 healthy people flagged out of 10,000, and the same test at 0.1, 1, 10 and 50 per cent prevalence gives 0.090, 0.500, 0.917 and 0.990 — the prior, not the accuracy, sets the scale. The odds form multiplies 1:4 by the likelihood ratio 4 to reach 1:1, and each head on the coin doubles the odds, so the chain 0.200, 0.333, 0.500 agrees with the batch formula at every count of heads from zero to five. Three boxes with priors 1/2, 1/6, 1/3 and likelihoods 1/3, 2/3, 1/2 give evidence 4/9 and posteriors 3/8, 1/4, 3/8, so the largest likelihood has the smallest posterior. The 2017 job question separates the two conditional directions through their shared joint 1/12 and ends at 4/5; the 2005 boxes give 4/19, and dropping a hypothesis from the denominator makes that 1, while omitting one of three elsewhere inflates 0.641 to 0.806 with the posteriors still adding to one. Four limits close the lesson: 0/0 evidence, overlapping hypotheses, one observation entered twice (0.500 against 0.333), and the prior as an input the theorem does not choose

runs.selected_unit: Section 1, Linear Algebra — the clause's last named item, LU decomposition, which the matrices lesson mentioned six times and developed nowhere
runs.selected_topic: LU decomposition: the recording rule and its four consequences. One rule — each multiplier used to clear an entry is kept in the position it cleared — and four consequences: the factorisation A = L U, the two triangular solves, the determinant as the product of the pivots, and the operation count. Plus the two conventions (Doolittle, Crout), the existence theorem with its assumption, the PA = LU repair, the L D L-transpose identity, and the Cholesky special case.
runs.selected_microtopic: the multiplier is entry over pivot, and the pivot is the trailing block's corner, not the original entry. The integer 3x3 [[2,1,-1],[-4,-1,3],[2,2,2]] gives multipliers -2, 1, 1 and factors that multiply back to all nine entries; the trailing block after step one is [[1,1],[1,3]], so m32 = 1 and u33 = 3 - 1 = 2. The GATE CSE 2022 system gives L32 = -1/2, U33 = -1/2 and x = (0, 2, -1) with y = (4, 3, 1/2) and a residual of exactly zero. The GATE CSE 2015 Set 1 matrix [[2,2],[4,9]] gives l22 = 5 under Crout and 1 under Doolittle, both pairs multiplying back to A. The 4x4 with pivots 4, 7/4, 12/7, 5/3 has det 20 by three routes: the pivot product, a cofactor expansion, and the fourth leading minor. [[1,1,1],[1,1,2],[1,2,2]] has minors 1, 0, -1 and det -1, so it is invertible and still has no LU without row swaps; the page swaps rows, verifies PA = LU, and reads det as 1 x 1 x 1 x (-1) = -1. Operation counts for n = 2..12 are measured by an instrumented triple loop and match (2/3)n^3 + (1/2)n^2 - (7/6)n exactly: 5, 19, 46, 90, 155, 245, 364, 516, 705, 935, 1210. At n = 10 that is 705 once against 190 per extra solve, so the crossover is at two right-hand sides, 1085 against 1410. The four GATE CSE 2025 Set 2 statements are decided as A, B, C true and D false, D refuted by the computed symmetric case P = [[4,2],[2,3]] giving L = [[1,0],[1/2,1]] and U = [[4,2],[0,2]], neither symmetric.

runs.selected_microtopic: three decisions and four counts. The block t1 = a*b, t2 = c*d, t3 = t1+t2, t4 = a*b, t5 = t4-t2 has 5 statements, 6 leaf occurrences and 5 operators but a DAG of 4 leaves and 4 operators: 11 instructions as a tree, 8 as a DAG. Sethi-Ullman labels (a-1)*(((b+c)/3)+d) 3; the exact search over evaluation orders returns 2 with immediates, 3 without, and the label with constants at 0 is also 2 — the 2017 keyed answer. Liveness on the GATE CSE 2013 Q49 block peaks at 4 ({a, d, e, x} at the if) with y live nowhere; the interference graph has 6 nodes and 10 edges, degrees 5, 1, 3, 4, 4, 3; greedy colouring uses 4, the chromatic number is 4, and the clique {a, c, d, e} proves it. With three registers the cheapest of the 63 spill sets is {d} at 1 reload plus 2 stores, while dropping b and x leaves the clique intact. Peephole removes 5 of 11 instructions, one per rule, agreeing on all 25 input pairs and reaching a fixed point.

runs.selected_microtopic: two questions, two lemmas, one table. The regular pumping lemma is searched as a game: a^n b^n leaves no surviving split at p = 1..8; {a^q : q prime} loses because pumping a^q by |y| exactly q times gives q(1+|y|), which is composite; and {a^i b^j c^k : i = 1 implies j = k} passes from p = 2 (129, 125, 117, 106 members tried, zero failures) while failing at p = 1 on 24 of 132 — at once the necessary-not-sufficient example and the too-small-pumping-length example. The CFL lemma defeats a^n b^n c^n across 6, 37, 121, 295, 605 and 1106 legal splits for n = 1..6, none surviving. Two three-state automata give union, intersection and difference as one 7-state product minimising to 5, complement at 3, concatenation at 7 minimising to 3, star at 3 (the same language, because it is already star-closed) and reversal at 4, each compared with its set-theoretic definition on all 255 strings of length <= 7. CFL union, concatenation and star are verified as grammars on all 1093 strings of length <= 6; intersection fails on the 2017 Set 1 witness pair a^n b^n c^m and a^m b^n c^n; complement fails by De Morgan. The [A,p,q] construction yields 5 nonterminals and 19 productions, verified on all 127 strings of length <= 6 against equal counts and even length. Emptiness is a productive fixed point, finiteness a reachable productive self-embedding nonterminal, membership linear or cubic, and universality, equivalence and ambiguity have no algorithm. Ambiguity is counted: 429 trees for a^8 under S -> S S | a.

runs.model: five machines: the 2025 paper machine (8 states, Mealy), the 1996 paper machine (4 states, Mealy), a twin machine built from two converging chains (7 states, Moore), and Moore and Mealy detectors for the same behaviour (3 and 2 states). Partition refinement is implemented from the definition, then checked three ways: an exact pair search over the product graph that decides equivalence of every pair, a brute-force comparison of the reduced machine against the original on all 511 input strings up to length eight from every state, and a well-definedness test that every member of a class prints the same output and lands in one class. Monotonicity of the passes, idempotence at the fixed point, and the n-1 pass bound are all checked

runs.model: Two simulations and one search, all in lesson.js. (a) A semaphore with the standard definition (decrement then block if negative; increment then wake if at most zero) and a resume-on-wake interpreter for both readers–writers solutions, so a process continues at the statement it blocked on; the safety invariant (never two writers, never a writer with a reader) is asserted after every statement of every script. (b) A breadth-first search over every reachable state of the philosophers table, with fork ownership derived from the philosopher labels rather than stored, so no inconsistent state can be built. (c) An independent wait-for graph built from the same states, whose cycle length must agree with the search. Results: naive 573 reachable and exactly 1 stuck (all five holding the first fork, wait-for cycle of 5, at most 2 eating); asymmetric 492 and 0; room of 4 permits 491 and 0; room of 5 permits 573 and 1, which is the check that the repair is n-1. Readers–writers: readcount 1/2/2/3/4 with wsem 0/0/-1/-1/-1; 20 readers inside against a queued writer; writer-first gives 1 queued on wsem and 19 on rmutex; readTry 0, wmutex -1, writecount 1, then readTry -1.

runs.model: seven programs, each a small state machine, searched exhaustively over every interleaving with each process running its loop twice: the naive read-then-store (52 states, 1 with two inside), test-and-set (135, 0), swap (425, 0), compare-and-swap (135, 0), the GATE 2012 fetch-and-add lock (318, and one state with nobody inside and the word at 1), the ticket lock (1201, 0) and the waiting-array algorithm (2352, 0). The 2012 defect is decided by a second forward search from the candidate state: 46 states visited, none with anybody inside. The exit scan is checked against its definition on all 256 combinations of process and waiting vector for two to five processes; the ticket invariant (whoever is inside holds the displayed ticket) and the ticket uniqueness invariant are checked at every reachable state; the spin cost is computed and compared with n(n-1)/2 at four and eight processes

runs.model: A finite evaluator for both calculi, plus the basic algebra beside it. An expression is a predicate together with the attribute list of its answer; evaluating it enumerates every candidate tuple over an AMBIENT DOMAIN, so the answer is a function of (expression, domain) — which is exactly the dependence safety forbids. That one decision makes safety measurable: evaluate over dom(P), then over dom(P) plus one fresh value that appears in no relation and no constant, and compare the two answer sets. Relational algebra is implemented independently (selection, projection, intersection, difference, theta join) so every equivalence claim is a set comparison. Reachability is evaluated the same way, by a two-hop expression over a chain, and compared with the n(n-1)/2 reachable ordered pairs. The 2001 options are evaluated over the whole question's ambient domain, with the per-formula verdict computed too and checked to agree on which option moves.

runs.model: The tabular method implemented twice on purpose. Route one, qm(), performs the passes a student writes: group by one-count, compare adjacent groups, dash the differing bit, tick both parents, collect unticked terms, repeat to a fixed point. Route two, maximal(), ignores the table entirely: it enumerates all 3^n cubes, keeps the implicants, and keeps those no other implicant contains. A check asserts the two sets are equal, so 'these are the prime implicants' is a measured claim rather than a quoted one. The covering half is written twice as well: petrick() forms one sum per column, multiplies, absorbs with X + XY = X, and reads the minimal products; minCovers() enumerates every subset of rows. A check asserts the two report the same minimal covers on all three functions. Every merge is checked for containment of both parents, every cube for 2^k coverage, and the absorption rule is checked in the reverse direction over all 64 assignments of the six decision variables.

runs.model: Four layers. The grammar types and their automata are data. The monotonic grammar is run by a bounded breadth-first derivation (65 rule applications, 41 distinct sentential forms, three terminal strings up to length 11) and its rules are checked one by one for shrinking. The regular and context-free pumping lemmas are run as exhaustive searches over exactly the splits each lemma allows, recording split counts and survivors. L1 and L2 are enumerated over i, j, k in 0..4 and the union identity 25 + 25 - 5 = 45 is checked; De Morgan is reproduced over the same universe to show that complement-plus-union yields the intersection. The closure and decidability tables are stored as data and their invariants (which cells fail, which counts rise) are asserted. The counting argument compares 2^52 - 1 languages against 2^51 - 2 machine descriptions. Two checks failed on the first run and were corrected: the closure table has three failing cells, not two (CFL twice and RE once), and decidability is not monotone along the chain (5, 3, 3, 5, 0), which became a teaching point rather than a hidden defect.

failures_found_and_fixed: The first draft of the stack representation used multi-character symbols in the replacement string, so the marker 'Z0' was pushed as two stack symbols and every run misbehaved: aaabbb ended in q1 after 6 steps and the whole language came out empty. Fixed by using single-character stack symbols and re-running the model, which then reported 3 accepted strings out of 127 as expected.

The first draft of the empty-stack scene claimed that a machine with one extra epsilon-branch accepts the same language while failing the determinism test. The brute-force enumeration refuted it: the branch accepted 9 strings where the language has 3, because the extra branch reached a final state. The branch was changed to enter a dead non-final state, which makes the claim true and keeps the teaching point; the model now reports the language unchanged and the violation still present.

The palindrome table was first written with the guess as a symbol-move, which made 'M_PAL has two choice violations and no epsilon conflict' true but left the machine accepting a superset of the palindromes under state-only acceptance. Rewritten with the guess as an epsilon-move (three conflicts of condition 2) plus a second table that writes the same guess as a symbol-move (two conflicts of condition 1), so both clauses of the definition are demonstrated on a real language and both machines accept exactly the palindromes.

Acceptance was briefly given an extra stack clause so that the palindrome tables could be compared on the right language. That made the swap analysis measure the clause rather than the stuckness and broke the claim that every wrong answer is a run that stopped early. Reverted to the textbook definition and every machine was redesigned to reach a final state only by popping the bottom marker.

research.implementation: The Linux kernel documentation, ext4 journal (jbd2), docs.kernel.org/filesystems/ext4/journal.html, read this run. It supplies the three phases (write the images, flush, write the commit record, then copy home and erase the commit record), the guarantee that a replay to the latest commit record makes a transaction atomic, the 10,240,000-block journal ceiling, the statement that ext4 by default journals only metadata so data blocks are not guaranteed consistent after a crash, and the three data modes.
research.mount_options: ext4.rst mount options and ext4(5), read this run. They supply the exact wording of data=journal, data=ordered marked as the default, and data=writeback with the statement that it 'can allow old data to appear in files after a crash and journal recovery', plus the 5-second default commit interval and the write-barrier default.
research.recovery: The Linux kernel documentation, The Linux Journalling API, docs.kernel.org/filesystems/journalling.html, read this run. It supplies the three-pass recovery: find the end of the log, assemble the list of revoke blocks, replay the un-revoked blocks. That is the source for the revoke-record edge case and for the 'three passes' scene.
research.design_paper: S. Tweedie, 'Journaling the Linux ext2fs Filesystem' (1998), read this run. It supplies the three journal block types (metadata, descriptor, header), the head and tail of the log with a sequence number in the header blocks, the rule that a transaction's log space is reusable only once every block it names has been written home, and the statement that a journal metadata block contains the entire contents of a block so the log stores images rather than deltas.
research.cited_not_fetched: Rosenblum and Ousterhout's log-structured file system paper and the ARIES paper are cited on the page for the journal-versus-LFS distinction and for the general redo/undo vocabulary. Neither was fetched this run; both claims are standard and are stated on the page without claiming a quotation. The one UNVERIFIED chip on the page marks the throughput judgement, which is an argument from sequential-write cost and not a measurement.

runs.model: Three layers of computation, all in lesson.js. (1) A block-level filesystem: an 8-block bitmap, a one-record inode table and 8 data blocks, three of them free but still holding a deleted file's bytes, and three transactions (create f = 2 metadata + 2 data blocks, unlink g = 2 metadata, append to f = 2 metadata + 1 data). Each transaction's writes are computed as the complete new IMAGE of each block, which is what a redo journal stores. (2) A schedule builder that turns the workload into an ordered list of write points under four disciplines: no journal, metadata-only writeback, metadata-only ordered, and full data journaling, giving 9, 24, 24 and 27 write points. (3) A crash harness that executes the first k write points for every k, recovers by scanning the journal for the last commit record and copying every logged image up to it, and checks four invariants — dangling reference, leaked block, aliased block, and bytes the file never wrote — on all 88 recovered images. Computed results the captions quote: no journal 6 of 10 crash points broken (3 metadata, 3 bytes) with the workload whole at 1; writeback 0 metadata and 7 byte failures, durable at 5 and intact at 2; ordered 0 and 0, intact at 4; full data journaling 0 and 0, intact at 5; the first bad crash point at k=1 with two leaked blocks and a dangling reference to block 0 at k=5; durability beginning at write point 6 for ordered and 4 for writeback; cost 2m+3 giving 5, 7, 11, 19, 35, 67 and 131 for m = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64; a 64-block journal holding 16 transactions of 2 metadata blocks and at most 62 metadata blocks; replay reading 64 blocks against 262,144 for a 1 GiB disk, a factor of 4,096; idempotence checked by comparing the recovered image twice against once; the abandoned second transaction discarded and matching the committed prefix with 8 log entries; and 3 of the 6 in-place orders of the append unsafe, exactly those writing the inode before the data block.

failures_found_and_fixed: Seven of the first fifty model checks failed, and every failure was an expectation of mine that the model refuted rather than a defect in the model. The unjournaled census breaks 6 of 10 crash points, not the 4 I had written; writeback exposes stale bytes at 7 of 25, not 3, because replay restores the metadata the moment the commit record is durable and the exposure therefore begins at the commit point rather than at the inode; writeback reaches durability at write point 4, earlier than ordered's 6, so the check that assumed a shared commit position was wrong; and writeback's workload is intact at only 2 crash points against 5 durable ones. Each check was rewritten to the measured value and the contrast between durable and intact was added as its own check, since it is the sharpest single statement on the page.

The discard check compared a recovered image against an unrecovered one, so it failed for the wrong reason. Rewritten to compare against the recovered image of the committed prefix, which is the property it names.

drawFrame threw 'Cannot read properties of undefined' during boot because sceneOf read LessonKit's scene list, which is empty until K.init runs. It now reads window.LESSON_TIMELINE.scenes, the same way the rest of the repo's lessons do.

Practice question 5 was first written with its arithmetic narrated in the answer ('Wait — compute carefully'). Rewritten to state the answer and the division once: 42 blocks per transaction, floor(4096/42) = 97.

runs.selected_microtopic: the whole microtopic, scoped as one table and two theorems: distance as a count of edges and the distance table built by BFS; eccentricity as a row maximum; diameter and radius as the maximum and minimum of the list; centre and periphery as the two arg-sets; self-centred graphs; the bounds ceil(d/2) <= r <= d with the triangle-inequality proof of the floor and C6, K4 and Petersen attaining the ceiling; the tree theorem r = ceil(d/2), one or two adjacent centres, and the centre as the middle of a diameter path; leaf peeling and its linear cost; the two-sweep diameter algorithm, exact on trees and wrong on the diamond; the height of a BFS tree against the diameter (GATE CSE 2025 Set 1 Q43); the square of a graph and diam(G^2) = ceil(d/2) (GATE CSE 2021 Set 1 Q20); and the three limits — a centre vertex on no diameter path, a disconnected graph with no finite eccentricity, and centre against centroid against median. The Wiener index, closeness and betweenness are excluded as outside the clause and are named as a later lesson in the Sources tab

runs.selected_topic: First-order resolution and unification: terms as trees, the most general unifier, Skolemisation, and the refutation rule that replaces a variable by a term instead of by an object
runs.selected_microtopic: a quantified sentence is not a ground clause and instantiating it may never terminate; a term as a finite tree and equality as node-for-node match; the substitution as a finite map that never touches constants, idempotent, associative and not commutative ({x/y} then {y/a} makes x into a, the other order leaves x alone); Robinson's walk to the first disagreement on f(x,g(y)) against f(a,g(b)), with the running substitution printed after each of the two bindings; the three failures — a clash, the occurs check (no finite term satisfies x = f(x), searched to depth four), and f(x,x) against f(a,b) which dies only after the first binding is applied; the most general unifier as the least commitment, tested by theta = sigma . theta2 on every unifier in a 12-term search space (12 for f(x,y) against f(y,a), 8 for p(x,f(x)) against p(y,z)); uniqueness up to renaming; matching as the one-way case; prenex form then Skolemisation with arity equal to the universals to the left (0 gives a constant, 1 gives f(x), 2 gives f(x,z)); equisatisfiability against equivalence, with 512 models of the originals failing their Skolem form; renaming apart, without which the occurs check silently refuses not P(x) with P(f(x)) or Q(x); the resolution step on not Man(x) or Mortal(x) with Man(s) giving Mortal(s) under {x/s}; factoring as a strengthening and not an equivalence, with the model that separates P(x) or P(y) or not R(x,y) from P(z) or not R(z,z); the two-step Socrates refutation as a tree with three leaves and one empty root; lifting and Herbrand as the completeness argument; and the three limits — semi-decidability by Church's theorem, no built-in equality, and syntactic matching
